title: Part 4, Chapter 4
paragraphs: Raskolnikov went straight to the house on the canal embankment where Sonia lived. It was an old green building of three storeys. He found the porter and obtained vague directions to the rooms of Kapernaumov, the tailor. Having found the entrance to a dark and narrow staircase in a corner of the courtyard, he climbed to the second floor and came out into a gallery that ran around the whole storey over the yard. While he wandered in the darkness, uncertain where to turn for Kapernaumov's door, a door opened three paces away. He mechanically took hold of it.
"Who's there?" a woman's voice asked uneasily.
"It's me—I've come to see you," Raskolnikov answered, and walked into the tiny entrance hall.
On a broken chair stood a candle in a battered copper candlestick.
"It's you! Good heavens!" Sonia cried weakly, and stood rooted to the spot.
"Which is your room? This way?" And Raskolnikov, trying not to look at her, hurried past.

A minute later Sonia came in with the candle, set down the candlestick, and stood before him, completely flustered, beside herself with agitation and apparently frightened by his unexpected visit. Color rushed to her pale face and tears came into her eyes. She felt sick and ashamed—and happy, too. Raskolnikov turned away quickly and sat on a chair by the table. He took in the room at a glance.

It was a large but extremely low-ceilinged room, the only one rented from the Kapernaumovs, whose rooms lay through a closed door in the left wall. On the opposite side, on the right wall, was another door, always locked, leading to the next apartment—a separate lodging. Sonia's room looked like a shed. It was an irregular quadrangle, and this gave it a grotesque appearance. A wall with three windows looking onto the canal ran at an angle, so that one corner was very acute and hard to see into without bright light. The other corner was disproportionately obtuse. There was almost no furniture in the big room: in the right-hand corner stood a bed, with a chair beside it nearest the door. A plain wooden table covered with a blue cloth stood against the same wall, near the door to the other apartment. Two rush-bottomed chairs stood by the table. Against the opposite wall, near the acute corner, was a small plain wooden chest of drawers, looking lost in the emptiness. The yellow, scratched, shabby wallpaper was black in the corners. It must have been damp and full of fumes in winter. Everything spoke of poverty; even the bed had no curtain.

Sonia looked silently at her visitor, who was scrutinizing her room so attentively and unceremoniously, and at last she began to tremble with terror, as though she stood before her judge and the arbiter of her fate.
"I'm late. It's eleven, isn't it?" he asked, still not raising his eyes.
"Yes," Sonia murmured. "Oh, yes it is," she added hastily, as though that offered a way out. "My landlady's clock has just struck—I heard it myself."
"I've come to you for the last time," Raskolnikov went on gloomily, though this was in fact his first visit. "I may not see you again."
"Are you—going away?"
"I don't know. Tomorrow."
"Then you won't come to Katerina Ivanovna's tomorrow?" Sonia's voice shook.
"I don't know. I'll know by morning. Never mind that—I came to say one thing."
He raised his brooding eyes to her and suddenly noticed that he was sitting while she had been standing before him the whole time.
"Why are you standing? Sit down," he said in a changed voice, gentle and friendly.
She sat down. He looked at her kindly, almost with compassion.
"How thin you are! What a hand! Completely transparent, like a dead hand."
He took her hand. Sonia smiled faintly.
"I've always been like this," she said.
"Even when you lived at home?"
"Yes."
"Of course you were," he added abruptly, and the expression of his face and the sound of his voice changed again suddenly.
He looked around the room once more.
"You rent this room from the Kapernaumovs?"
"Yes."
"They live there, through that door?"
"Yes. They have another room like this one."
"All in one room?"
"Yes."
"I'd be afraid in your room at night," he observed darkly.
"They're very good people, very kind," Sonia answered, still seeming dazed, "and all the furniture—everything—is theirs. They're very kind, and the children often come to see me too."
"They all stammer, don't they?"

"Yes. He stammers and he's lame. His wife too—well, not exactly stammers, but she can't speak clearly. She's a very kind woman. He used to be a house serf. And there are seven children—only the eldest stammers; the others are just sickly—they don't stammer. But how did you hear about them?" she added with some surprise.
"Your father told me everything. He told me all about you—how you went out at six and came back at nine, and how Katerina Ivanovna knelt by your bed."
Sonia was embarrassed.
"I thought I saw him today," she whispered hesitantly.
"Whom?"
"Father. I was walking in the street, near the corner, about ten o'clock. He seemed to be walking ahead of me. It looked exactly like him. I wanted to go to Katerina Ivanovna."
"You were out walking in the streets?"
"Yes," Sonia whispered abruptly, again overcome with confusion and looking down.
"Katerina Ivanovna used to beat you, I suppose?"
"Oh no, what are you saying! No!" Sonia looked at him almost with dismay.
"You love her, then?"

"Love her? Of course!" Sonia said with plaintive emphasis, clasping her hands in distress. "Oh, you don't—if you only knew! You see, she's like a child. Her mind has come unhinged, from grief. But how clever she used to be! How generous! How kind! You don't understand—you don't understand!"

Sonia said this in something like despair, wringing her hands in anguish. Her pale cheeks flushed, her eyes held a look of pain. She was clearly stirred to the depths, longing to speak, to advocate, to express something. A kind of insatiable compassion showed in every feature of her face.

"Beat me! How can you say that? Good heavens, beat me! And even if she did—what of it? You know nothing about it. She's so unhappy—oh, so unhappy! And sick. She demands justice; she's pure. She has such faith that there must be justice everywhere, and she expects it. If you tortured her, she wouldn't do wrong. She can't see that it's impossible for people to be perfectly just, and she's angry about it. Like a child! She's good!"
"And what will become of you?"
Sonia looked at him inquiringly.
"They're all on your shoulders, you know. They were before, too. Your father came to you begging for drink money. Well, what happens now?"
"I don't know," Sonia said mournfully.
"Will they stay where they are?"
"I don't know. They're behind on the rent, and the landlady apparently said today that she wants them out. Katerina Ivanovna says she won't stay another minute."
"Where does she get her nerve? She's counting on you?"

"Oh, no, don't talk that way. We're one family; we live as one." Sonia was agitated again, even angry, like a small bird ruffling its feathers. "And what could she do? What could she do?" she went on, growing heated and excited. "How she cried today! Her mind is unhinged—haven't you noticed? One minute she's fussing like a child, making sure everything will be perfect tomorrow for the lunch. The next she's wringing her hands, spitting blood, weeping; then suddenly she starts banging her head against the wall in despair. Then she's comforted again. She's pinning all her hopes on you; she says you'll help her now, and that she'll borrow some money and go back to her hometown with me and open a boarding school for gentlemen's daughters, with me to run it, and we'll start a wonderful new life. She kisses me and hugs me and comforts me—and she has such faith, such faith in these fantasies! You can't contradict her. All day she's been washing, cleaning, mending. She dragged the washtub into the room with her feeble hands and sank onto the bed gasping. We went to the shops this morning to buy shoes for Polenka and Lida—their old ones are worn to nothing. But the money we'd reckoned wasn't enough, not nearly enough. She picked out such dear little boots—she has good taste, you know. And right there in the shop she burst into tears in front of the shopkeepers because she didn't have enough. It was heartbreaking to watch."
"Well, after that I can understand how you live," Raskolnikov said with a bitter smile.

"And don't you feel sorry for them? Don't you?" Sonia flew at him. "I know you gave your last penny, though you hadn't even seen them. If you'd seen everything—oh God! And how many times, how many times I've brought her to tears! Just last week—yes! Only a week before he died. I was cruel! And how often I've done it! I've been wretched thinking about it all day!"
Sonia wrung her hands as she spoke, in the pain of remembering.
"You were cruel?"

"Yes—I! I went to see them," she continued, weeping, "and father said, 'Read to me, Sonia, my head aches—read me something. Here's a book.' He had a book from Andrey Semyonovich Lebeziatnikov, who lives there—he always gets hold of such odd books. And I said, 'I can't stay.' I'd really come to show Katerina Ivanovna some collars. Lizaveta, the peddler, had sold me some collars and cuffs cheap—pretty, new, embroidered ones. Katerina Ivanovna liked them very much. She put them on, looked at herself in the mirror, and was delighted. 'Give them to me, Sonia,' she said, 'please!' She wanted them so much. When would she ever wear them? They just reminded her of her old happy days. She admired herself in the mirror—she has no decent clothes at all, hasn't had for years! And she never asks anyone for anything—she's too proud, she'd sooner give everything away. But these she asked for—she loved them so much. And I didn't want to give them. 'What use are they to you, Katerina Ivanovna?' I said. I actually said that to her! I shouldn't have. She gave me such a look. She was so hurt—so hurt by my refusal. It was painful to see. And she wasn't hurt about the collars, but because I refused. I could see that. If only I could take it all back, change those words! Oh, if I—but none of that matters to you."
"Did you know Lizaveta, the peddler?"
"Yes. Did you?" Sonia asked in some surprise.
"Katerina Ivanovna is consumptive, advanced consumption. She'll die soon," Raskolnikov said after a pause, without answering her question.
"Oh no, no, no!"
And Sonia unconsciously clutched both his hands, as though begging that she should not die.
"But it will be better if she does."
"No, not better! Not at all better!" Sonia echoed in dismay.
"And the children? What can you do then, except take them in yourself?"
"Oh, I don't know!" Sonia cried, almost in despair, putting her hands to her head.
The thought had clearly crossed her mind many times before; he had only stirred it up again.
"And what if even now, while Katerina Ivanovna is still alive, you fall ill and are taken to the hospital—what then?" he pressed, without mercy.
"How can you! That can't happen!"
Sonia's face twisted with terrible fear.

"Can't happen?" Raskolnikov went on with a harsh smile. "You're not insured against it, are you? And then what happens to them? They'll be on the streets, all of them. She'll cough and beg and bang her head against a wall, the way she did today, and the children will cry. She'll collapse, be taken to the police station, then to the hospital—she'll die—and the children—"
"Oh no! God will not let it happen!" burst at last from Sonia's overburdened heart.
She listened, gazing at him imploringly, hands clasped in mute entreaty, as though it all depended on him.
Raskolnikov got up and began pacing the room. A minute passed. Sonia stood with her arms hanging, her head bowed in terrible dejection.
"Can't you save anything? Put something aside for a rainy day?" he asked, stopping suddenly before her.
"No," Sonia whispered.
"Of course not. Have you tried?" he added, almost ironically.
"Yes."
"And it didn't work! Of course not! No need to ask."
He resumed pacing. Another minute passed.
"You don't earn money every day?"
Sonia was more flustered than ever, and color rushed to her face.
"No," she whispered with painful effort.
"It'll be the same with Polenka, no doubt," he said suddenly.
"No! No! It can't be! No!" Sonia cried aloud in desperation, as though she'd been stabbed. "God wouldn't allow anything so terrible!"
"He allows it to happen to others."
"No, no! God will protect her! God!" she repeated, beside herself.
"But perhaps there is no God at all," Raskolnikov answered with a kind of malicious pleasure, laughing as he looked at her.
Sonia's face changed suddenly. A tremor passed over it. She looked at him with unutterable reproach, tried to speak, but couldn't, and broke into bitter, bitter sobbing, hiding her face in her hands.
"You say Katerina Ivanovna's mind is unhinged. Your own mind is unhinged," he said after a short silence.

Five minutes passed. He paced up and down without looking at her. At last he went to her. His eyes glittered. He placed both hands on her shoulders and looked straight into her tearful face. His eyes were hard, feverish, piercing; his lips twitched. Suddenly he dropped to his knees and kissed her foot. Sonia shrank back from him as from a madman. And indeed he looked like one.
"What are you doing?" she whispered, turning pale, and a sudden anguish gripped her heart.
He stood up at once.

"I wasn't bowing to you—I was bowing to all human suffering," he said wildly, and walked to the window. "Listen," he added, turning to her a minute later. "I told a certain insolent man just now that he wasn't worth your little finger—and that I did my sister honor by having her sit beside you."
"Oh, you said that to them! And in front of her?" Sonia cried, frightened. "Sit beside me! An honor! But I'm—dishonorable! Oh, why did you say that?"

"It wasn't because of your dishonor and your sin that I said it, but because of your great suffering. But you are a great sinner, that's true," he added, almost solemnly, "and your worst sin is that you've destroyed and betrayed yourself for nothing. Isn't that terrible? Isn't it terrible that you live in this filth you loathe so, while knowing all along—you need only open your eyes—that you're not helping anyone, not saving anyone from anything? Tell me," he demanded, almost in a frenzy, "how this shame and degradation can exist in you side by side with other, opposite, holy feelings? It would be better, a thousand times better and wiser, to throw yourself into the water and end it all!"
"But what would become of them?" Sonia asked faintly, gazing at him with anguished eyes—but apparently not at all surprised by his suggestion.

Raskolnikov looked at her strangely. He read it all in her face: she had already had that thought, perhaps many times, and in earnest, had considered in her despair how to end it all—so earnestly that now she barely wondered at his words. She hadn't even noticed the cruelty in them. The significance of his reproaches and his peculiar attitude toward her shame she obviously hadn't grasped either—that too was clear to him. But he could see how monstrously the thought of her disgraceful, shameful position had been tormenting her, and for a long time. "What," he thought, "what could have stopped her from putting an end to it?" Only then did he fully realize what those poor little orphans and that pathetic, half-crazed Katerina Ivanovna, banging her head against the wall in her consumption, meant for Sonia.

Nevertheless, it was equally clear that with her character and the education she had somehow received, she could not possibly remain as she was. The question still confronted him: how could she have endured this position for so long without going out of her mind, since she couldn't bring herself to jump into the water? He knew, of course, that Sonia's case was exceptional—though unhappily not unique or even infrequent—but that very uniqueness, her trace of education, her previous life, might have been expected to destroy her at the first step on that revolting path. What sustained her? Surely not depravity. All that degradation had obviously only touched her mechanically; not a drop of true corruption had seeped into her heart. He could see that. He saw through her as she stood before him.
"Three paths lie before her," he thought: "the canal, the madhouse, or finally sinking into the kind of depravity that numbs the mind and turns the heart to stone."
The last seemed most likely to him. But he was a skeptic, he was young, abstract, and therefore cruel, and so he couldn't help believing the final outcome was the most probable.

"But can that really be true?" he exclaimed to himself. "Can this creature, who still preserves the purity of her spirit, be consciously dragged at last into that sink of filth and vice? Has the process already begun? Can it be that she's only endured it so far because vice has begun to seem less loathsome? No, no—that can't be!" he cried, as Sonia had done before. "No, what's kept her from the canal is the idea of sin—and them, the children. And if she hasn't gone out of her mind—but who says she hasn't? Is she in her senses? Can one talk and reason as she does? Can she sit on the edge of the abyss into which she's sliding and refuse to listen when told of the danger? Is she waiting for a miracle? No doubt she is. And isn't that itself a kind of madness?"
He clung stubbornly to that thought. Indeed, he preferred that explanation to any other. He began watching her more intently.
"So you pray to God a great deal, Sonia?" he asked.
Sonia was silent. He stood beside her, waiting for an answer.
"What would I be without God?" she whispered rapidly, forcibly, glancing at him with suddenly blazing eyes and squeezing his hand.
"Ah, so that's how it is!" he thought.
"And what does God do for you?" he asked, probing further.
Sonia was silent for a long time, as though she couldn't answer. Her thin chest heaved with emotion.
"Be quiet! Don't ask! You don't deserve to know!" she cried suddenly, looking at him sternly and wrathfully.
"That's it, that's it," he repeated to himself.
"He does everything," she whispered quickly, looking down again.

"So that's the way out! That's the explanation," he decided, scrutinizing her with eager curiosity and a new, strange, almost morbid feeling. He studied that pale, thin, irregular, angular little face, those soft blue eyes that could flash with such fire, such stern energy, that small body still trembling with indignation and anger—and it all seemed to him more and more strange, almost impossible. "She's a religious fanatic!" he repeated to himself.

There was a book lying on the chest of drawers. He had noticed it each time he paced the room. Now he picked it up and examined it. It was the New Testament, in Russian, bound in leather, old and worn.
"Where did you get this?" he called across the room.
She still stood in the same place, three steps from the table.
"It was brought to me," she answered, reluctantly, without looking at him.
"Who brought it?"
"Lizaveta. I asked her for it."
"Lizaveta! How strange!" he thought.
Everything about Sonia seemed stranger and more extraordinary to him with every passing moment. He carried the book to the candle and began turning the pages.
"Where is the story of Lazarus?" he asked suddenly.
Sonia stared stubbornly at the floor, not answering. She was standing sideways to the table.
"Where is the raising of Lazarus? Find it for me, Sonia."
She stole a glance at him.
"You're not looking in the right place. It's in the fourth gospel," she whispered sternly, without looking at him.
"Find it and read it to me," he said. He sat down with his elbow on the table, leaned his head on his hand, and looked away, bracing himself to listen.
"In three weeks they'll welcome me in the madhouse! I'll probably be there, if I'm not somewhere worse," he muttered to himself.
Sonia approached the table hesitantly, not quite trusting his request. She picked up the book, however.
"Haven't you read it?" she asked, looking across the table at him.
Her voice was growing sterner.
"Long ago. When I was at school. Read!"
"And haven't you heard it in church?"
"I—no. Do you go often?"
"N-no," Sonia whispered.
Raskolnikov smiled.
"I see. And you won't go to your father's funeral tomorrow?"
"Yes, I will. I was at church last week too—I had a requiem service."
"For whom?"
"For Lizaveta. She was killed with an axe."
His nerves tightened further. His head began to spin.
"Were you friends with Lizaveta?"
"Yes. She was good. She used to come—not often—she couldn't. We read together and talked. She will see God."
These last words sounded strange to his ears. And here was something new: the mysterious meetings with Lizaveta, and both of them—religious maniacs.
"I'll become one myself soon! It's contagious!"
"Read!" he cried irritably and insistently.
Sonia still hesitated. Her heart was pounding. She hardly dared read to him. He looked at the "poor lunatic" almost with exasperation.
"Why? You don't believe?" she whispered softly, almost breathlessly.
"Read! I want you to," he insisted. "You used to read to Lizaveta."
Sonia opened the book and found the place. Her hands were shaking; her voice failed her. Twice she tried to begin and couldn't get out the first syllable.
"Now a certain man was sick, named Lazarus, of Bethany—" she forced herself to read at last, but on the third word her voice broke like an overstrained string. Her breath caught.

Raskolnikov understood in part why Sonia could not bring herself to read to him, and the more he understood, the more roughly and insistently he demanded it. He understood all too well how painful it was for her to expose and reveal what was her own. He understood that these feelings were truly her secret treasure, perhaps kept for years, perhaps from childhood, while she lived with an unhappy father and a grief-maddened stepmother amid starving children and ugly abuse and reproaches. But at the same time he now knew—knew for certain—that although it filled her with dread and suffering, she had a tormenting desire to read, to read to him, now, whatever might come of it. He read this in her eyes, could see it in her intense emotion. She mastered herself, controlled the spasm in her throat, and continued reading the eleventh chapter of St. John. She reached the nineteenth verse:
"And many of the Jews came to Martha and Mary, to comfort them concerning their brother."
"Then Martha, as soon as she heard that Jesus was coming, went and met Him: but Mary sat still in the house."
"Then said Martha unto Jesus, Lord, if Thou hadst been here, my brother had not died."
"But I know, that even now, whatsoever Thou wilt ask of God, God will give it Thee."
She stopped again, shamefacedly aware that her voice would quiver and break.
"Jesus said unto her, Thy brother shall rise again."
"Martha saith unto Him, I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day."
"Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection and the life: he that believeth in Me, though he were dead, yet shall he live."
"And whosoever liveth and believeth in Me shall never die. Believest thou this?"
"She saith unto Him,"
(Drawing a painful breath, Sonia read distinctly and forcefully, as though making a public confession of faith:)
"Yea, Lord: I believe that Thou art the Christ, the Son of God, Which should come into the world."
She paused, glanced up at him quickly, but controlled herself and went on reading. Raskolnikov sat without moving, elbows on the table, eyes turned away. She read to the thirty-second verse.
"Then when Mary was come where Jesus was, and saw Him, she fell down at His feet, saying unto Him, Lord, if Thou hadst been here, my brother had not died."
"When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews also weeping which came with her, He groaned in the spirit, and was troubled,"
"And said, Where have ye laid him? They said unto Him, Lord, come and see."
"Jesus wept."
"Then said the Jews, Behold how He loved him!"
"And some of them said, Could not this Man, which opened the eyes of the blind, have caused that even this man should not have died?"

Raskolnikov turned and looked at her with emotion. Yes, he had known it! She was trembling in a real physical fever. He had expected it. She was approaching the story of the greatest miracle, and a feeling of immense triumph was overtaking her. Her voice rang like a bell; triumph and joy gave it power. The lines danced before her eyes, but she knew the words by heart. At the last verse—"Could not this Man, which opened the eyes of the blind..."—she dropped her voice and passionately reproduced the doubt, the reproach and censure of the blind, disbelieving Jews, who in another moment would fall at His feet as though struck by thunder, sobbing and believing. "And he—he too is blinded and unbelieving; he too will hear, he too will believe—yes, yes! Now, this very moment!" she dreamed, trembling with joyful anticipation.
"Jesus therefore again groaning in Himself cometh to the grave. It was a cave, and a stone lay upon it."
"Jesus said, Take ye away the stone. Martha, the sister of him that was dead, saith unto Him, Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days."
She emphasized the word four.
"Jesus saith unto her, Said I not unto thee, that, if thou wouldest believe, thou shouldest see the glory of God?"
"Then they took away the stone from the place where the dead was laid. And Jesus lifted up His eyes, and said, Father, I thank Thee that Thou hast heard Me."
"And I knew that Thou hearest Me always: but because of the people which stand by I said it, that they may believe that Thou hast sent Me."
"And when He thus had spoken, He cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth."
"And he that was dead came forth."
(She read loudly, cold and trembling with ecstasy, as though she were seeing it before her eyes.)
"Bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go."
"Then many of the Jews which came to Mary, and had seen the things which Jesus did, believed on Him."
She could read no more. She closed the book and rose quickly from her chair.

"That is all about the raising of Lazarus," she whispered severely and abruptly, and stood motionless, turned away, not daring to raise her eyes to him. She still trembled feverishly. The candle stub flickered in its battered candlestick, dimly lighting the poverty-stricken room where the murderer and the harlot had so strangely come together over the eternal book. Five minutes or more passed.

"I came to talk about something," Raskolnikov said aloud, frowning. He got up and went to Sonia. She raised her eyes to him in silence. His face was particularly stern and held a kind of savage determination.
"I've abandoned my family today," he said, "my mother and sister. I'm not going to see them. I've broken with them completely."
"Why?" Sonia asked, amazed. Her recent meeting with his mother and sister had left a deep impression she could not analyze. She received his news almost with horror.
"I have only you now," he added. "Let us go together. I've come to you. We are both cursed—let us go together!"
His eyes glittered "as though he were mad," Sonia thought.
"Go where?" she asked in alarm, involuntarily stepping back.
"How should I know? I only know it's the same road. I know that for certain, and nothing more. The same goal!"
She looked at him and understood nothing. She knew only that he was terribly, infinitely unhappy.
"None of them will understand if you tell them, but I have understood. I need you—that's why I've come to you."
"I don't understand," Sonia whispered.

"You'll understand later. Haven't you done the same? You too have transgressed—you had the strength to transgress. You took your own life, you destroyed a life—your own. It's all the same! You might have lived in spirit and reason, but you'll end up in the Haymarket. But you won't be able to bear it, and if you stay alone you'll go mad, like me. You're already like a mad creature. So we must go together, on the same road! Let us go!"
"Why? Why are you saying all this?" Sonia said, strangely and violently agitated by his words.

"Why? Because you can't stay like this—that's why! You have to face things squarely at last and stop crying like a child, insisting God won't allow it. What will happen if you're really taken to the hospital tomorrow? She's mad and consumptive; she'll die soon. And the children? Do you mean to tell me Polenka won't come to grief? Haven't you seen children at street corners, sent out by their mothers to beg? I've found out where those mothers live and how they live. Children can't remain children in such places! A seven-year-old is already vicious and a thief. Yet children are the image of Christ: 'Theirs is the kingdom of heaven.' He commanded us to honor and love them. They are the future of humanity."
"What can be done? What can be done?" Sonia repeated, weeping hysterically and wringing her hands.

"What can be done? Smash what must be smashed, once and for all, that's all—and take the suffering upon yourself. What, you don't understand? You'll understand later. Freedom and power—and above all, power! Over all trembling creation, over the whole anthill! That's the goal—remember that! This may be my farewell message. Perhaps it's the last time I'll speak to you. If I don't come tomorrow, you'll hear about everything—and then remember these words. And someday later, in years to come, perhaps you'll understand what they meant. If I do come tomorrow, I'll tell you who killed Lizaveta. Goodbye."
Sonia started with terror.
"Do you know who killed her?" she asked, frozen with horror, staring at him wildly.

"I know, and I'll tell you—you and only you. I've chosen you. I'm not coming to ask your forgiveness—simply to tell you. I chose you long ago for this—when your father talked about you, when Lizaveta was still alive. Goodbye. Don't shake hands. Tomorrow!"
He left. Sonia stared after him as at a madman. But she herself felt like one and knew it. Her head was spinning.

"Good heavens! How does he know who killed Lizaveta? What did those words mean? It's terrifying!" But at the same time the idea did not enter her mind—not for a single moment! "Oh, he must be terribly unhappy! He's abandoned his mother and sister. Why? What happened? What did he have in mind? What did he say to her? He kissed her foot and said—yes, he said it clearly—that he couldn't live without her. Oh, merciful heavens!"

Sonia spent the whole night in fever and delirium. She kept jumping up, weeping, wringing her hands, then sinking back into fitful sleep, dreaming of Polenka, Katerina Ivanovna, Lizaveta, the reading from the Gospel—and him, with his pale face and burning eyes, kissing her feet, weeping.

On the other side of the door on the right, which separated Sonia's room from Madame Resslich's apartment, was a room that had long stood empty. A card was posted on the gate and a notice in the windows overlooking the canal, advertising it for rent. Sonia had long been accustomed to the room being vacant. But all that time, Mr. Svidrigaïlov had been standing at the door of the empty room, listening. When Raskolnikov left, he stood still, thought for a moment, then went on tiptoe to his own room, which adjoined the empty one. He fetched a chair and carried it noiselessly to the door leading to Sonia's room. The conversation had struck him as interesting and remarkable, and he had enjoyed it immensely—so much so that he brought the chair so he wouldn't have to endure the inconvenience in the future, tomorrow for instance, of standing for a whole hour. He could listen in comfort.
